title: Supplement Promises
question: Special supplements and powders can reliably boost a healthy person's immune system above its normal working level.
correctExplanation: False. The system is already finely regulated, and no supplement has been shown to push a healthy one measurably above its normal function.
incorrectExplanation: It is false. Deficiency correction helps people who lack a nutrient, but adding more to a well-nourished body does not upgrade the defences. Regulation, not raw power, is the goal.
lessonContent:
Healthy systems are regulated, not maximized.
Correcting a deficiency differs from adding a surplus.
Marketing thrives on the image of a dial to turn up.
Sleep, movement, and nutrition support normal function best.

title: Live Virus Worry
question: Most routine vaccines contain live, disease-causing pathogens that can give the recipient the disease they prevent.
correctExplanation: False. Most vaccines use killed pathogens, harmless fragments, or a single protein recipe, none of which can cause the infection.
incorrectExplanation: It is false. Modern vaccines overwhelmingly teach the immune system without a real infection — inactivated, fragment, or genetic-instruction designs. A few attenuated vaccines use weakened forms that healthy immune systems control easily.
lessonContent:
Vaccination teaches without requiring the disease.
Different designs use killed, fragment, or coded instructions.
Weakened forms are controlled by functioning immunity.
Knowing which design is used answers most risk questions.
Share this: identify the type of one vaccine you received and how it works.

title: Bacteria Killers
question: Antibiotics are effective against viral infections such as the common cold and influenza.
correctExplanation: False. Antibiotics target bacterial machinery, and viruses do not use that machinery at all.
incorrectExplanation: It is false. A virus hijacks your own cells, so drugs aimed at bacterial structures have nothing to attack. Overusing antibiotics anyway breeds resistance without helping the patient.
lessonContent:
Drugs act on specific targets, not on illness in general.
Viruses and bacteria are structurally different.
Mismatched drugs waste effort and create resistance.
Diagnosis comes before prescription for good reason.

title: The Useful Fever
question: Fever is usually a coordinated immune response that can help fight infection, not simply a malfunction to be suppressed at any cost.
correctExplanation: True. Raising body temperature is an active defence that can slow some pathogens and speed immune activity.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. Fever is a strategy the body deliberately runs, not a breakdown. Managing comfort matters, but treating every rise in temperature as an emergency can work against the defences.
lessonContent:
Symptoms are often strategies, not accidents.
Fever reflects an active regulatory response.
Comfort measures and fever treatment are different goals.
Distinguishing defence from damage guides good decisions.

title: Overreacting Immunity
question: Allergies indicate an immune system that is dangerously weak and unable to defend the body.
correctExplanation: False. Allergies come from an overreaction to harmless substances, which is a targeting error rather than a strength deficit.
incorrectExplanation: It is false. The reaction itself shows a vigorous response aimed at the wrong target. Calling it weakness misreads a mismatch as a shortfall, which leads to the wrong advice.
lessonContent:
Immune problems can be misdirected rather than deficient.
Targeting errors and weakness require opposite treatments.
Descriptive precision prevents bad advice.
Vigour aimed wrongly is still vigour.

title: Remembering Invaders
question: After an infection, some immune cells persist specifically to recognise that same pathogen if it returns.
correctExplanation: True. Memory cells survive long after the fight, enabling a faster and stronger response on the next encounter.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. Immunological memory is the whole principle behind both natural protection and vaccination. The system keeps a trained reserve rather than starting from scratch.
lessonContent:
Defences can be trained and retained.
Memory cells make the second response faster.
Vaccination borrows this same mechanism.
Reserves reduce cost on future encounters.

title: Repeat Colds
question: People can catch colds again and again because many different viruses cause them, and protection against one may be brief.
correctExplanation: True. Hundreds of virus types cause colds, and immunity to each is narrow, so repeat infections are normal.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. Renewed colds are not evidence of a broken immune system but of an enormous variety of culprits. Narrow, sometimes short-lived protection leaves plenty of room for the next virus.
lessonContent:
Variety defeats broad immunity.
Protection is usually pathogen-specific.
Repeat illness is often arithmetic, not weakness.
Breadth of threats explains apparent fragility.

title: Soap and Spread
question: Regular handwashing with soap reduces the spread of many common infections.
correctExplanation: True. Soap physically removes microbes from skin, and hand contact is a major route of transmission.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. Soap does not need to kill anything — lifting and rinsing away the microbes is enough. Interrupting the route of transfer beats fighting the infection after it starts.
lessonContent:
Prevention can outwork treatment.
Physical removal is often enough to break transmission.
Simple measures beat exotic ones when they cut the route.
Contact is a major channel for pathogens.

title: Friendly Fire
question: In autoimmune conditions, the immune system mistakenly attacks the body's own tissues.
correctExplanation: True. Recognition errors turn the defences against self, causing damage in joints, glands, nerves, or organs.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. Autoimmunity is a targeting failure, not a lack of power. That distinction explains why some treatments suppress the immune response rather than strengthen it.
lessonContent:
Recognition errors can turn defences inward.
Treatment sometimes means calming an overactive system.
Weakness and misdirection need opposite responses.
Diagnosis identifies which failure is occurring.
Share this: explain tonight why an autoimmune disease is not a weak immune system.

title: Symptomless Strength
question: A perfectly strong immune system would mean never experiencing symptoms like swelling, redness, or fever.
correctExplanation: False. Many symptoms are produced by the immune response itself, so a silent system is not necessarily a superior one.
incorrectExplanation: It is false. Swelling brings repair cells, redness brings blood flow, and fever shifts conditions against pathogens. Suppressing them can remove the defence along with the discomfort.
lessonContent:
Symptoms are often the sound of the response working.
Symptom-free and well-protected are different things.
Reducing discomfort can conflict with healing.
Observe before assuming a symptom is purely damage.

title: Two Cell Families
question: T cells and B cells are both types of white blood cells central to immune defence.
correctExplanation: True. They are the main actors of adaptive immunity: B cells make antibodies while T cells coordinate and destroy infected cells.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. Both arise from bone marrow and then specialise, forming the trained branch of the immune system. Their division of labour explains why responses can be both targeted and coordinated.
lessonContent:
Division of labour exists inside immunity.
One family makes weapons, another directs strikes.
Specialisation enables precise responses.
Bone marrow supplies the shared origin.
Share this: name tonight the two roles of the adaptive defence families.

title: First Milk
question: Breast milk passes protective antibodies from mother to infant, providing temporary immune help.
correctExplanation: True. Antibodies in early milk give newborns borrowed protection while their own immune system matures.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. The protection is temporary because the antibodies are borrowed rather than produced by the child. It bridges a vulnerable period until the infant's own defences develop.
lessonContent:
Protection can be transferred between individuals.
Borrowed defence is temporary by nature.
Timing matters most during developmental gaps.
Cooperation is built into mammalian biology.
Share this: note tonight one way protection is shared across a family.

title: Once and Done
question: Someone who has had chickenpox is usually protected against catching it again.
correctExplanation: True. Surviving the infection generally produces long-lasting immunity to that virus.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. Immune memory keeps the response ready for decades in most people, which is why second cases are rare. The virus can still lie dormant and reappear later as shingles, a different phenomenon.
lessonContent:
Some infections grant durable protection.
Memory can last decades without re-exposure.
Dormancy and reinfection are separate ideas.
Distinguishing them prevents confusion.
Share this: explain tonight the difference between catching it again and it waking up.

title: Mega Doses
question: Taking very large daily doses of vitamin C reliably prevents the common cold in the general population.
correctExplanation: False. Large trials find no meaningful prevention in ordinary adults, though the vitamin supports normal function at adequate levels.
incorrectExplanation: It is false. The vitamin is essential, but more is not better beyond sufficiency, and megadoses show no reliable preventive effect. Correcting a deficiency still matters for those who lack it.
lessonContent:
Essential nutrients have sufficiency thresholds.
More is not the same as better beyond that point.
Effect sizes from large trials beat vivid anecdotes.
Distinguish supporting normal function from boosting it.

title: Old Saying
question: The folk advice to feed a cold and starve a fever has solid scientific support.
correctExplanation: False. The saying has no reliable evidence behind it, and adequate hydration and nutrition support recovery from either.
incorrectExplanation: It is false. Rhyming sayings survive by memorability, not by trials. Eating well and drinking enough help in both cases; withholding food during illness is not a treatment.
lessonContent:
Memorable advice is not the same as correct advice.
Rhyme and tradition carry no evidential weight.
Basics like hydration serve most illnesses.
Test proverbs against evidence before following them.
Share this: pick one folk remedy tonight and check whether any trial supports it.

title: Numbers and Protection
question: Measuring antibody levels alone always gives a complete and accurate picture of how well protected a person is.
correctExplanation: False. Antibody counts miss cellular memory and vary between people and assays, so they are one clue rather than the whole story.
incorrectExplanation: It is false. Someone with modest antibody levels may still respond quickly thanks to memory cells, and results differ by test. Protection is a system property, not a single number.
lessonContent:
Complex systems resist single-number summaries.
Different branches of immunity support each other.
One measurement can mislead when others are ignored.
Prefer system-level evidence over isolated figures.

title: Community Shield
question: High vaccination rates in a population can protect people who cannot be vaccinated themselves.
correctExplanation: True. When enough people are immune, transmission chains break and vulnerable individuals face far less exposure.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. The protection is indirect but real: fewer carriers means fewer opportunities for the pathogen to reach those who lack their own defence. This is why coverage levels matter collectively.
lessonContent:
Immunity has effects beyond the individual.
Breaking transmission chains protects the vulnerable.
Collective outcomes depend on coverage thresholds.
Individual and public benefits can align.
Share this: explain tonight how someone unvaccinated can still benefit from others' shots.

title: All Microbes Guilty
question: All bacteria are harmful to human health and ideally should be eliminated.
correctExplanation: False. Trillions of bacteria live on and inside us, and many support digestion, skin defence, and vitamin production.
incorrectExplanation: It is false. Only a minority cause disease, while resident communities compete with invaders and train the immune system. Wiping them out indiscriminately damages the host as well.
lessonContent:
Microbial life is mostly commensal, not hostile.
Resident communities help exclude invaders.
Indiscriminate killing harms the host environment.
Ecological thinking fits the body well.
Share this: note tonight one living thing inside you that helps you.

title: Probiotic Claims
question: Probiotic products are proven to prevent or cure most common infectious diseases.
correctExplanation: False. Evidence supports a few narrow uses, and broad disease-prevention claims outrun the trials.
incorrectExplanation: It is false. Some strains help specific conditions like certain antibiotic-related diarrhoea, but the blanket promises do not survive scrutiny. Strain specificity is central and often ignored by marketing.
lessonContent:
Biological effects are strain-specific.
Narrow evidence does not license broad claims.
Markets reward sweeping promises; trials do not.
Ask which strain and which condition before believing.

title: The Retracted Study
question: The claim that childhood vaccines cause autism originates from a fraudulent, later retracted study.
correctExplanation: True. The original paper was retracted, its author lost his licence, and large studies have found no link.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. Millions of children across multiple countries have been studied, and no connection appears. The anxiety persists because the initial claim spread widely before being dismantled.
lessonContent:
Retracted findings can outlive their correction.
Large multi-country studies are powerful evidence.
Fraud can seed decades of damage.
Check whether a claim's source still stands.
Share this: trace tonight the origin of one health scare you have heard.

title: Second Encounter
question: Immune memory is one reason why some diseases rarely recur in the same person.
correctExplanation: True. Remembering pathogens lets the body mount a fast, strong response that often stops infection before symptoms start.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. This prepared reserve is why immunity can be lifelong for some diseases and why vaccines work at all. Speed on the second encounter is the entire advantage.
lessonContent:
Remembered defences act before symptoms appear.
Speed is the key benefit of prior exposure.
Not every pathogen triggers lasting memory.
Timing distinguishes protection from infection.
Share this: explain tonight why a vaccinated person may never notice exposure.

title: Healing Cuts
question: Immune activity contributes to wound healing, not only to fighting infections.
correctExplanation: True. Immune cells clear debris and release signals that recruit repair cells to rebuild tissue.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. Healing involves coordination between microbial defence and tissue construction, which is why immune problems can delay recovery. The system is a builder as well as a guard.
lessonContent:
Defence and repair share machinery.
Clearing debris is part of rebuilding.
Immune problems can slow physical healing.
Systems often serve more than one purpose.
Share this: observe tonight how a small cut swells then rebuilds.

title: Yearly Shots
question: Seasonal influenza vaccines are updated regularly largely because the virus changes its surface features over time.
correctExplanation: True. Drifting surface proteins let the virus evade existing immunity, so the recipe is revised each season.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. The virus accumulates changes that older antibodies recognise poorly, which is why last year's shot may not match this year's strains. Updating follows the virus's evolution, not commercial habit.
lessonContent:
Pathogens evolve to evade existing defences.
Matching a moving target requires updates.
Old protection weakens as the target changes.
Evolution explains recurring public-health tasks.
Share this: note tonight why vaccine recipes can change from year to year.

title: Chilly Weather
question: Cold weather by itself directly causes the viral infections we call colds.
correctExplanation: False. Viruses cause colds; cold weather only creates conditions and behaviours that help them spread.
incorrectExplanation: It is false. Temperature does not manufacture viruses, though it may favour transmission and drive people indoors together. The cause and the seasonal pattern are separate facts.
lessonContent:
Patterns of disease differ from causes of disease.
Correlation with seasons is not causation.
Behaviour changes transmission routes.
Separate mechanism from circumstance.
Share this: explain tonight why winter raises risk without causing the germ.

title: Weak or Overactive
question: An autoimmune disease means the immune system is too weak to defend the body properly.
correctExplanation: False. Autoimmunity is a recognition error in which a vigorous response targets the body itself.
incorrectExplanation: It is false. The system is active — sometimes aggressively so — but aimed at the wrong targets. This is why some treatments dampen the response rather than stimulate it.
lessonContent:
Direction of error matters as much as magnitude.
Weakness and misdirection need opposite care.
Treatment logic follows the failure mode.
Diagnosis determines which response is appropriate.
Share this: sort tonight one immune condition into weak or misdirected.
